newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon said meeting with rating agencies.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon said meeting with rating agencies.

text.p: Defense giant Raytheon Corp has been meeting with bond rating agencies to defend its possible acquisition of Hughes Electronics Corp's missile and radar business, people familiar with the deal said Wednesday.

Both Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's Corp put the Lexington, Mass.-based company's debt rating under review for a possible downgrade after Raytheon agreed to buy Texas Instruments Inc defense assets for $2.95 billion last week.

An S&P spokesman said there was no meeting Wednesday and Moody's said it does not comment on meetings with companies. A Raytheon spokesman also declined to comment. But analysts who follow both companies said Raytheon has been meeting with the rating agencies to seek to avoid a downgrade.

"Raytheon is meeting with the bond rating people. There's some hint that they're considering taking them to junk bond status and Raytheon doesn't want that," said one analyst. "But it looks like the basic deal has been handed out to them so they can really review it."

J.P. Morgan analyst Roger Threlfall said Hughes parent General Motors Corp has also been meeting with the U.S. Internal Revenue Service over its proposed Hughes asset sale. He said Raytheon's meetings with the rating agencies and GM's meeting with the IRS are signs "that things are moving along."

Threlfall said GM proposed to the IRS that it transfer its "letter" shares to assets shares in a move similar to one the Detroit giant used in its spinoff of Texas-based Electronic Data Systems Corp last year.
Under the terms of that tax-free deal each share of GM Class E stock was exchanged for one share of new EDS common stock.
But Threlfall noted the terms of this deal are considerably different. "Delco, telecom and space (all segments of Hughes) are not part of this transaction," he said.
GM spokesmen could not be reached for comment.

Raytheon is in a battle with rival Northrop Grumman Corp for the Hughes assets, widely regarded as one of the last big trophies in the quickly consolidating defense industry. The firms are believed to have submitted bids between $9.5 billion and $10.4 billion.

"Price is only a secondary concern at this point," JSA Research analyst Paul Nesbitt said. "Raytheon's earnings are much larger. They have much more flexibility financially. Northrop would have to issue six billion (dollars worth) of shares of stock, which is more stock than they currently have outstanding."
